warmup.q: In a RecursiveTask, compute() splits the range into left and right, then runs left.fork(); long l = left.join(); long r = right.compute(); return l + r;. On a 4-worker pool, how much faster than one thread is it?
options: About 4 times faster, because every split forks a task
About 2 times faster, because only the top split runs in parallel
About the same speed as one thread
It deadlocks, because a worker joins its own task
warmup.why: join() right after fork() waits for the left half before the right half starts, so the two halves of every split run one after the other. The worker usually just pops the task it forked and runs it itself, which is legal and doesn't deadlock. Put right.compute() between the fork and the join and the same code gets close to 4 times faster.

sections.h: RecursiveTask: split until the piece is small, then loop
sections.html:
ForkJoinPool (JDK 7) is a pool built for one shape of work: a big CPU job that splits itself into smaller jobs of the same kind. You describe the job as a RecursiveTask<V>, which returns a value, or a RecursiveAction, which doesn't. Both have one method to write, compute(), and it nearly always has this shape:

Java
class SumTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    static final int THRESHOLD = 10_000;
    final long[] a; final int from, to;

    SumTask(long[] a, int from, int to) { this.a = a; this.from = from; this.to = to; }

    @Override
    protected Long compute() {
        if (to - from <= THRESHOLD) {                   // 1. small enough: just loop
            long sum = 0;
            for (int i = from; i < to; i++) sum += a[i];
            return sum;
        }
        int mid = (from + to) >>> 1;                    // 2. split
        SumTask left = new SumTask(a, from, mid), right = new SumTask(a, mid, to);
        left.fork();                                    // 3. let another worker take the left half
        long r = right.compute();                       // 4. do the right half here
        return left.join() + r;                         // 5. then collect the left half
    }
}

long total = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new SumTask(amounts, 0, amounts.length));
Kotlin
class SumTask(val a: LongArray, val from: Int, val to: Int) : RecursiveTask<Long>() {
    override fun compute(): Long {
        if (to - from <= THRESHOLD) {                   // 1. small enough: just loop
            var sum = 0L
            for (i in from until to) sum += a[i]
            return sum
        }
        val mid = (from + to) ushr 1                    // 2. split
        val left = SumTask(a, from, mid)
        val right = SumTask(a, mid, to)
        left.fork()                                     // 3. let another worker take the left half
        val r = right.compute()                         // 4. do the right half here
        return left.join() + r                          // 5. then collect the left half
    }

    companion object { const val THRESHOLD = 10_000 }
}

val total = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(SumTask(amounts, 0, amounts.size))

The threshold is the one number you have to choose. Too big, and there are only a few pieces, so some workers sit idle at the end. Too small, and the cost of creating and scheduling task objects eats the gain. The ForkJoinTask Javadoc gives a very rough rule: a task should do more than 100 and less than 10,000 basic computational steps. Then measure.

ForkJoin tasks are for CPU work on data you already have in memory: summing a ledger, sorting, searching, transforming a big array. They should not block on I/O or locks, for reasons the last section shows.

try.title: Change the threshold
steps: Run WorkStealingDemo. It totals fees over 2,000,000 ledger entries, first on one thread, then on a ForkJoinPool with 4 workers. Note the speed-up and how many leaves each worker ran.
Run it with -Pargs="right 500", then with -Pargs="right 1000000". Before each run, predict the number of leaves and how many workers will have any.

Args: [right|wrong] [threshold]. */ public class WorkStealingDemo { static final Map<String, LongAdder> LEAVES = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); static long fee(long amountCents) { long h = amountCents; for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) h = (h * 31 + i) % 1_000_003; // stands in for real fee rules return amountCents * 29 / 1_000 + 30 + h % 2; } static final class Fees extends RecursiveTask<Long> { final long[] amounts; final int from, to, threshold; final boolean wrong; Fees(long[] amounts, int from, int to, int threshold, boolean wrong) { this.amounts = amounts; this.from = from; this.to = to; this.threshold = threshold; this.wrong = wrong; } @Override protected Long compute() { if (to - from <= threshold) { LEAVES.computeIfAbsent(Thread.currentThread().getName(), k -> new LongAdder()).increment(); long sum = 0; for (int i = from; i < to; i++) sum += fee(amounts[i]); return sum; } int mid = (from + to) >>> 1; Fees left = new Fees(amounts, from, mid, threshold, wrong); Fees right = new Fees(amounts, mid, to, threshold, wrong); left.fork(); if (wrong) { long leftFees = left.join(); // waits for the left half before starting the right one return leftFees + right.compute(); } long rightFees = right.compute(); // works on the right half while the left one can be stolen return left.join() + rightFees; } } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean wrong = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("wrong"); int threshold = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 50_000; long[] amounts = new long[2_000_000]; for (int i = 0; i < amounts.length; i++) amounts[i] = 100 + (i * 7919L) % 250_000; long s0 = System.nanoTime(); long expected = 0; for (long a : amounts) expected += fee(a); // one thread, for comparison System.out.printf("one thread: %,d ms%n", (System.nanoTime() - s0) / 1_000_000); try (ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(4)) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long total = pool.submit(new Fees(amounts, 0, amounts.length, threshold, wrong)).join(); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; new TreeMap<>(LEAVES).forEach((thread, n) -> System.out.printf("%-24s %4d leaves%n", thread, n.sum())); System.out.printf("%s order, threshold %,d: %,d ms, %d steals, same total: %b%n", wrong ? "wrong" : "right", threshold, ms, pool.getStealCount(), total == expected); } } }

try.expect: With the default threshold of 50,000, all four workers run some of the 64 leaves, and the pool finishes about 3 to 4 times faster than one thread if your machine has 4 free cores. With 500 there are 4,096 leaves and it is still fast, a little slower from the extra tasks. With 1,000,000 there are only 2 leaves, so only 2 workers ever get work and the speed-up drops to about 2.

sections.h: Work stealing, and why fork, compute, join is the only good order
sections.html:
A ThreadPoolExecutor has one shared queue. A ForkJoinPool gives every worker its own double-ended queue, a deque. fork() pushes the task onto the top of the current worker's deque. The worker also pops from the top, so it always works on the task it forked most recently: the smallest one, whose data is still in its cache.

A worker whose deque is empty becomes a thief. It picks another worker and takes the task at the bottom of that worker's deque. That is the oldest task, forked highest up in the recursion, so it is the biggest piece of work available. The thief splits it on its own deque and stays busy for a long time. That's why WorkStealingDemo reports only a handful of steals for 64 leaves.

join() doesn't simply park the thread. If the task is still on the worker's own deque, the worker pops it and runs it. If a thief took it, the worker helps by running other pending tasks while it waits. A fork/join pool doesn't need a spare thread for every task that is waiting on another.

Now the order. Fork one half, compute the other on this thread, and only then join:

Java
left.fork();                    // the left half becomes stealable
long r = right.compute();       // this thread works while a thief can take the left half
return left.join() + r;
Kotlin
left.fork()                     // the left half becomes stealable
val r = right.compute()         // this thread works while a thief can take the left half
return left.join() + r

Swap the last two steps, left.fork(); left.join(); right.compute(), and the worker waits for the left half before it even starts the right one. The two halves of every split run one after the other. left.compute() + right.compute() is the same thing written honestly: sequential code with extra objects. Both still give the right total, which is why the bug survives code review. invokeAll(left, right) is the library's shortcut for the correct order.

sections.h: Parallel streams run on the common pool, along with everything else
sections.html:
list.parallelStream() splits its source into pieces and runs them as fork/join tasks on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). The calling thread takes part too: in SharedStateDemo, main shows up next to the common pool workers.

The common pool has availableProcessors() - 1 threads by default (you can change it with -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism). It is one pool for the whole JVM. Every parallel stream uses it, every CompletableFuture async method without an executor uses it (lesson 6 of this track), and from JDK 25 so does scheduling on the common pool (lesson 5). Whatever runs there competes with all of that.

Three mistakes cover most parallel stream bugs.

  • Writing to shared state races. forEach(p -> list.add(p)) on an ArrayList, or forEach(x -> total[0] += x), runs the same read-modify-write races as any other threads. The demo loses about half the ids, and the sum comes out wrong by billions. Let the stream build the result: toList(), collect(...), sum(), reduce(...). Each thread works on its own piece, and the stream combines the pieces at the end.
  • Order isn't kept. forEach on a parallel stream runs in whatever order the threads get to the elements. toList() and forEachOrdered keep the source order, at some cost.
  • Too little work makes it slower. Splitting, scheduling and combining cost time. A stream of 1,000 cheap elements is faster sequential. Sources that split badly, such as a LinkedList, Stream.iterate or lines from a file, give the pool little to share out. That comes from how a stream splits its source. An array or an ArrayList splits in half by index, in one step, and each half can go to another worker. A LinkedList has no middle to jump to. Its Spliterator, the object that does the splitting, walks the list from the front and copies the next 1,024 elements into an array, then the next 2,048, and so on, all on the one thread that splits. Measure both versions, ideally with JMH (the OpenJDK harness for microbenchmarks), before you keep parallel().

refs.title: java.util.stream package: parallelism and side effects (Java SE 25 API)

sections.h: Blocking calls starve the common pool
sections.html:
A ForkJoinPool tries to keep about parallelism threads running. When one of them blocks in Thread.sleep, a socket read or a JDBC call, the pool normally doesn't know, and that thread is simply gone until the call returns. With 7 workers on an 8-core pod, seven slow issuer lookups in a parallel stream take every common pool thread in the JVM.

StarvationDemo runs four rounds of 300 ms lookups in a parallel stream. As soon as all the threads are busy, another thread submits a task that should take microseconds, through supplyAsync with no executor. It waits about 1.2 seconds, until the lookups are nearly done. In a service, that tiny task is somebody else's request.

The fix is to keep I/O off the common pool. Run blocking calls on an executor built for waiting: a bounded pool sized for the downstream, or virtual threads, which the next track covers. Then combine the results with CompletableFuture. In the demo's io mode, the lookups finish in about 300 ms and the tiny task waits about 2 ms.

There is also a patch for code you can't move. ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(blocker) tells the pool "this worker is about to block", and the pool may start a spare thread to keep its parallelism up. CompletableFuture uses it internally when a pool thread calls join(). In the demo's managed mode, spare workers appear (with names like commonPool-worker-10) and both numbers look good again. It is still a patch: every blocked call costs a whole platform thread, and the spares are capped.

You may read that a parallel stream started inside customPool.submit(...) runs on customPool. It does today, but it is how the implementation behaves, not something the specification promises. Don't build on it.

code.title: StarvationDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l08; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.stream.IntStream; /** Blocking BIN lookups in a parallel stream while a tiny task needs the common pool. Args: [blocking|managed|io]. */ public class StarvationDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static final int PARALLELISM = ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism(); static final AtomicInteger STARTED = new AtomicInteger(); static final CountDownLatch ALL_BUSY = new CountDownLatch(1); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static void lookup() { if (STARTED.incrementAndGet() == PARALLELISM + 1) ALL_BUSY.countDown(); // the common pool and main are all busy sleep(300); // a remote call } static void managedLookup() { try { // tells the pool this worker is about to block, so it can start a spare thread ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(new ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker() { boolean done; @Override public boolean block() { lookup(); done = true; return true; } @Override public boolean isReleasable() { return done; } }); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "blocking"; int lookups = (PARALLELISM + 1) * 4; // four rounds of work for the common pool and main log(mode + ": common pool parallelism " + PARALLELISM + ", " + lookups + " lookups of 300 ms"); Thread fx = new Thread(() -> { try { ALL_BUSY.await(); // start once the lookups are under way } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } long t = System.nanoTime(); String who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).join(); // a tiny task log("tiny task waited " + (System.nanoTime() - t) / 1_000_000 + " ms, then ran on " + who); }); fx.start(); if (mode.equals("io")) { try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(lookups)) { List<CompletableFuture<Void>> calls = IntStream.range(0, lookups) .mapToObj(i -> CompletableFuture.runAsync(StarvationDemo::lookup, io)) .toList(); calls.forEach(CompletableFuture::join); } } else { boolean managed = mode.equals("managed"); IntStream.range(0, lookups).parallel().forEach(i -> { if (managed) managedLookup(); else lookup(); }); } log("all lookups done"); fx.join(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: StarvationDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l08 import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.stream.IntStream import kotlin.concurrent.thread private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private val parallelism = ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism() private val started = AtomicInteger() private val allBusy = CountDownLatch(1) private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg)) private fun lookup() { if (started.incrementAndGet() == parallelism + 1) allBusy.countDown() // the common pool and main are all busy Thread.sleep(300) // a remote call } private fun managedLookup() { // tells the pool this worker is about to block, so it can start a spare thread ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(object : ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker { var done = false override fun block(): Boolean { lookup() done = true return true } override fun isReleasable() = done }) } /** Blocking BIN lookups in a parallel stream while a tiny task needs the common pool. Args: [blocking|managed|io]. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "blocking" val lookups = (parallelism + 1) * 4 // four rounds of work for the common pool and main log("$mode: common pool parallelism $parallelism, $lookups lookups of 300 ms") val fx = thread { allBusy.await() // start once the lookups are under way val t = System.nanoTime() val who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { Thread.currentThread().name }.join() // a tiny task log("tiny task waited ${(System.nanoTime() - t) / 1_000_000} ms, then ran on $who") } if (mode == "io") { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(lookups).use { io -> val calls = (0 until lookups).map { CompletableFuture.runAsync(::lookup, io) } calls.forEach { it.join() } } } else { val managed = mode == "managed" IntStream.range(0, lookups).parallel().forEach { if (managed) managedLookup() else lookup() } } log("all lookups done") fx.join() }

try.expect: In the default mode the lookups take about 1.2 s (four rounds of 300 ms on the common pool plus main), and the tiny task waits about as long, because every common pool thread is asleep. With io the lookups take about 300 ms and the tiny task waits a few milliseconds. With managed the pool adds spare workers, so both drop again, and the tiny task runs on one of the extra threads.

analogy: A fork/join pool is a team splitting a stack of 2,000 invoices to check. Each clerk keeps a personal pile. When you split your pile, you put half on top of it and keep working on the other half yourself. A clerk with nothing to do walks over and takes the bottom of somebody else's pile, which is the biggest bundle, so nobody has to walk over often. The analogy breaks when a clerk picks up the phone to a supplier for ten minutes: in an office you'd notice and share out the pile, but the pool usually can't tell a thread is waiting, so that clerk's desk just stands empty.
world: Good fork/join work in a payment service is CPU work on data already in memory: totalling fees over a day's ledger extract, building a settlement file, deduplicating a batch of idempotency keys, sorting a big reconciliation set. Bad work is anything that calls out: an issuer lookup, a database query or a Kafka send inside a parallelStream(). On an 8-core Quarkus pod that has 7 common pool threads shared by the whole service, and the stall shows up as unrelated CompletableFuture timeouts somewhere else. When you do turn on parallel(), check the container's CPU limit, because availableProcessors() follows it and a 2-CPU pod gets a common pool of one worker.
mistake: The most common mistake is putting blocking calls in a parallel stream: ids.parallelStream().map(client::fetch).toList(). It looks like a free speed-up and it is one in a laptop test, where nothing else needs the common pool. In production the calls hold the common pool's few threads, and every parallel stream and every executor-less CompletableFuture in the JVM waits behind them. People reach for it because parallelStream() is the shortest way to say "do these at once". For I/O, say it with an executor: supplyAsync(() -> client.fetch(id), io) for each id, then join them all at the edge.

compare.title: Divide and conquer: RecursiveTask vs coroutines

java.title: CountOver.java (ForkJoinPool)
java.html: class CountOver extends RecursiveTask<Integer> { final long[] a; final long limit; final int from, to; CountOver(long[] a, long limit, int from, int to) { this.a = a; this.limit = limit; this.from = from; this.to = to; } @Override protected Integer compute() { if (to - from <= 10_000) { int n = 0; for (int i = from; i < to; i++) if (a[i] > limit) n++; return n; } int mid = (from + to) >>> 1; CountOver left = new CountOver(a, limit, from, mid); CountOver right = new CountOver(a, limit, mid, to); left.fork(); // stealable int r = right.compute(); // work here return left.join() + r; // then collect } } int flagged = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new CountOver(amounts, 500_000, 0, amounts.length));

kotlin.title: CountOver.kt (kotlinx.coroutines)
kotlin.html: suspend fun countOver(a: LongArray, limit: Long, from: Int, to: Int): Int = if (to - from <= 10_000) { (from until to).count { a[it] > limit } } else coroutineScope { val mid = (from + to) ushr 1 val left = async { countOver(a, limit, from, mid) } // like fork() val right = countOver(a, limit, mid, to) // like compute() left.await() + right // like join() } val flagged = runBlocking(Dispatchers.Default) { countOver(amounts, 500_000, 0, amounts.size) }

compare.note: Kotlin can extend RecursiveTask exactly like Java (the Kotlin WorkStealingDemo does). The coroutine version keeps the same shape and the same order rule: start the left half with async, compute the right half in place, then await. Two things differ. Dispatchers.Default is kotlinx.coroutines' own shared thread pool, sized to the number of cores (at least two); it is not the common ForkJoinPool, so it doesn't compete with parallel streams. And await() suspends the coroutine instead of helping with other tasks, so the thread goes back to the dispatcher. Blocking calls are just as wrong on Dispatchers.Default as on the common pool; they belong on Dispatchers.IO.

worked.title: Speed up a nightly fee report without breaking it

steps.say: The report totals fees per merchant over 4 million payments. Someone made it parallel. Before reading on, find what breaks.
steps.code: Map<String, Long> feesByMerchant = new HashMap<>(); payments.parallelStream().forEach(p -> feesByMerchant.merge(p.merchant(), fee(p), Long::sum)); // one HashMap, many threads

alt.html: val feesByMerchant = HashMap<String, Long>() payments.parallelStream().forEach { p -> feesByMerchant.merge(p.merchant, fee(p), Long::plus) // one HashMap, many threads }

steps.say: Many threads call merge on one HashMap. That loses updates, and a resize under concurrent writes can corrupt the map. Let the stream build the result instead: with groupingBy, each thread fills its own partial map and the stream merges them at the end.
steps.code: // 1. CPU work only, and the stream owns the result Map<String, Long> feesByMerchant = payments.parallelStream() .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Payment::merchant, Collectors.summingLong(this::fee)));

alt.html: // 1. CPU work only, and the stream owns the result val feesByMerchant: Map<String, Long> = payments.parallelStream() .collect(Collectors.groupingBy({ it.merchant }, Collectors.summingLong(::fee)))

steps.say: Next someone wants merchant names in the report, from a service that takes 20 ms per call. Calling it inside the parallel stream would block the common pool for 4 million calls. There are only about 3,000 merchants, so look the names up after the aggregation, once each, on an IO pool.
steps.code: // 2. IO goes to a pool built for waiting, once per merchant Map<String, CompletableFuture<String>> names = feesByMerchant.keySet().stream() .collect(Collectors.toMap(id -> id, id -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> merchants.name(id), io))); // 3. wait at the edge: the report job's own thread may block names.forEach((id, name) -> report.line(name.join(), feesByMerchant.get(id)));

alt.html: // 2. IO goes to a pool built for waiting, once per merchant val names = feesByMerchant.keys.associateWith { id -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ merchants.name(id) }, io) } // 3. wait at the edge: the report job's own thread may block names.forEach { (id, name) -> report.line(name.join(), feesByMerchant.getValue(id)) }

steps.say: Last question: is parallel() worth keeping? Time both versions on production-sized data, with JMH or at least a few warm runs. With a cheap fee and a few thousand payments the sequential stream often wins. Keep parallel() only where the numbers say so, and remember that the pod's CPU limit sets the common pool's size.

lab.title: Fork a ledger, then fix two parallel streams
steps: Run the tests. All six fail.

Write LedgerFees.compute. If to - from <= threshold, loop over the range and add up fees.feeCents(amounts[i]). Otherwise split at the midpoint into two new LedgerFees (use the private constructor), fork one half, compute the other, then join.
Fix ParallelPitfalls.flaggedIds: keep parallelStream(), drop the shared list, and let the stream collect the ids with map(Payment::id).toList().
Fix ParallelPitfalls.issuers: start one supplyAsync(() -> lookup.issuer(bin), io) per BIN, collect the futures, then join them into the result map on the calling thread.
Run the tests until all six pass, then run them twice more.
hints: runsHalvesInParallel makes the first fee on each thread wait until a second thread arrives. If it times out, your two halves ran one after the other: compute the second half before you join the first.
(from + to) >>> 1 is a midpoint that can't overflow.

In issuers, create every future before you join any of them. A single stream that maps to supplyAsync and then to join handles one element at a time, so each lookup finishes before the next one starts, and issuersRunsAllAtOnce times out.
lab.done: All six tests in ForkJoinTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A RecursiveTask from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a RecursiveTask<Long> that finds the largest amount in a long[], with a threshold of 10,000, and the line that runs it on the common pool. Then compare. Is your compute() between the fork() and the join()?

answer.title: MaxAmount.java
answer.html: class MaxAmount extends RecursiveTask<Long> { final long[] a; final int from, to; MaxAmount(long[] a, int from, int to) { this.a = a; this.from = from; this.to = to; } @Override protected Long compute() { if (to - from <= 10_000) { long max = Long.MIN_VALUE; for (int i = from; i < to; i++) max = Math.max(max, a[i]); return max; } int mid = (from + to) >>> 1; MaxAmount left = new MaxAmount(a, from, mid); MaxAmount right = new MaxAmount(a, mid, to); left.fork(); long r = right.compute(); return Math.max(left.join(), r); } } long max = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new MaxAmount(amounts, 0, amounts.length));

alt.title: MaxAmount.kt
alt.html: class MaxAmount(val a: LongArray, val from: Int, val to: Int) : RecursiveTask<Long>() { override fun compute(): Long { if (to - from <= 10_000) { var max = Long.MIN_VALUE for (i in from until to) max = maxOf(max, a[i]) return max } val mid = (from + to) ushr 1 val left = MaxAmount(a, from, mid) val right = MaxAmount(a, mid, to) left.fork() val r = right.compute() return maxOf(left.join(), r) } } val max = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(MaxAmount(amounts, 0, amounts.size))

recap: A RecursiveTask splits its range until it is below a threshold, then loops. The ForkJoinTask Javadoc suggests roughly 100 to 10,000 basic steps per leaf.
Fork one half, compute the other on this thread, then join. Joining before computing runs every split one half after the other.
Each worker pushes and pops at the top of its own deque; idle workers steal the oldest, biggest task from the bottom of someone else's. join() helps instead of just waiting.
Parallel streams run on ForkJoinPool.commonPool() plus the calling thread: cores minus one workers, shared with every default-executor CompletableFuture in the JVM.
Never write to shared state from a parallel stream. Let toList(), collect, sum or reduce build the result.
Blocking calls starve the common pool. Run I/O on an executor built for waiting; ManagedBlocker is a patch for code you can't move.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate how work stealing keeps four workers busy on a recursive ledger sum, and why left.fork(); left.join(); right.compute() gets no speed-up even though it forks.
explain.answer: Each worker has its own deque. When a task splits, it forks one half onto the top of its worker's deque and works on the other half itself. Idle workers steal from the bottom of a busy worker's deque, where the oldest and largest piece sits, split it on their own deques, and so the work spreads across all four with only a few steals. join either runs the task itself, if nobody stole it, or helps with other work while it waits. With fork immediately followed by join, the worker waits for the left half before it starts the right half. Even if a thief takes the left half, the forking worker just waits for it, so the two halves of every split never overlap and the total time is about the same as one thread.

deeper.html:
The virtual thread scheduler that the next track covers is also a ForkJoinPool, a separate instance from the common pool. JEP 444 describes it as a work-stealing ForkJoinPool that operates in FIFO mode. FIFO mode exists for tasks that are submitted and never joined, like events or messages: you get it with the asyncMode argument of the four-argument ForkJoinPool constructor, and each worker then takes its own tasks oldest first instead of newest first.

The common pool has a few more knobs, all system properties read once when the pool starts: java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism, .threadFactory, .exceptionHandler and .maximumSpares, which caps the spare threads that managedBlock can add. Calling close() or shutdown() on the common pool does nothing, so library code can't switch it off by accident.

Why does availableProcessors() - 1 make sense? Because the thread that calls invoke or starts a parallel stream works too. Seven workers plus the caller keep eight cores busy. It also means that on a 2-CPU container the common pool has one worker, and before JDK 25 that was enough for CompletableFuture to stop using it (lesson 6).

Parallel streams don't use RecursiveTask internally. They use CountedCompleter, a ForkJoinTask that counts pending subtasks and runs a completion action when the count reaches zero, so no thread ever waits in join(). You rarely need to write one yourself, but it is the reason a parallel stream can split deep trees without stacking up joins.
